content: Sentinel centers will have the autonomy to determine how they make information publicly accessible. Ideally, this should be achieved through peer-reviewed publications available in open-source formats. However, the World Health Organization (WHO) strongly encourages direct and real-time data sharing with national public health authorities to foster collaboration in public health efforts. The application of attributable fraction data to national mortality figures, particularly in the context of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, necessitates close collaboration between sentinel centers and public health officials responsible for national mortality estimates. This collaboration may require formal agreements, such as a memorandum of understanding. National mortality estimates related to hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis D virus (HDV), and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections will only be considered official if they are prepared with the full cooperation of national public health authorities. In most countries, this process will involve formal clearance procedures. This project involves establishing a new surveillance system, which is one of the three pillars of a national surveillance system for hepatitis as recommended by WHO. The surveillance of sequelae does not qualify as research under the definition of an ethics committee, as the results are not generalizable across countries. Nevertheless, investigators will ensure the protection of human subjects, as outlined below. Patients will not derive specific benefits from this project, as the tests involved are part of their routine medical care for cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma. If a patient included in the protocol lacks certain information in their medical record that should have been part of standard assessment practices, clinicians may consider collecting the information if it benefits the patient. To minimize harm and ensure confidentiality, only identifier codes (ID codes) will be used on data collection forms. A list of enrolled patients will be maintained to track ID codes and any expressed desire to opt out. This list will be securely stored, either under lock and key or on a high-security, password-protected computer. No additional blood collection will be required for this surveillance. If a clinician deems certain information unnecessary and it is missing from the medical record, it will be marked as such. The diagnostic procedures for which data will be collected are part of routine medical care for patients with cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma. No additional information or blood tests will be collected for this surveillance. Upon admission, patients will be informed via an information sheet that the center is participating in a surveillance activity. This sheet will explain that the information will be collected as part of routine clinical care and used for surveillance without any identifying information. No additional data will be gathered beyond what is required for routine medical care. The information sheet will also explain how patients can opt out. If a patient chooses to opt out, their information will be deleted from the patient list. The information sheet must meet the following conditions: Patients must be made aware of its existence. Sufficient information must be provided to patients. Patients must be informed that they can withdraw their data. A genuine opportunity to object must be offered. The project involves setting up a new surveillance activity using data collected as part of routine care. Depending on national regulations, ethics committee clearance may be required. The protocol will be submitted to WHO and other relevant ethics committees to determine the appropriate level of review (e.g., exemption, expedited approval, or full review). The protocol has already been approved by an independent scientific review team composed of external scientific experts with no connection to the project. Expected outputs of the project include: A representative sample of patients with cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Estimates of the proportion of patients with cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma who are infected with HBV, HCV, or both. Expected outcomes include: Improved national mortality estimates after applying attributable fraction data to mortality figures. Enhanced capacity for surveillance of HBV and HCV infections among patients with cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Lessons learned for scaling up the project. Establishment of a community of practice and partnerships with clinicians and laboratory specialists to support testing, treatment, and in-vitro diagnostics during biomarker surveys. Cost considerations for the project include: Initial training workshops. Support for investigators in data collection. Biomarker testing kits (e.g., anti-HCV and hepatitis B surface antigen [HBsAg] kits for 250 patients, with sequential testing to reduce costs). Support for data analysis and presentation. Final dissemination and evaluation workshops. Future perspectives include the extension of pilot projects to generate high-quality, sustainable information. Centers of clinical excellence will serve as resource partners, enabling engagement in testing and treatment activities, including quality aspects of in-vitro diagnostics.
